\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling~\cite{snell2024scaling} for LLM-based code repair depends critically on verification: given $K$ candidate patches, a verifier must rank and filter them by predicted correctness. Full execution verification is reliable but expensive---running test suites against each candidate costs \$1--3 and several minutes at repository scale, making it prohibitive for large $K$. Execution-free alternatives must therefore balance accuracy, diagnostic granularity, and computational cost. Yet the choice of \emph{how} to formulate the verification task---what the model predicts and in what format---has received surprisingly little attention.

Two dominant paradigms have emerged for execution-free verification, each with distinct limitations. \textbf{Generation-based simulation}~\cite{meta2025cwm,ding2025selfexecution}: Code World Models predict the execution output string for each test, then derive pass/fail verdicts by exact match against expected outputs. This approach works well when outputs are short and structurally simple, but suffers from two systematic failure modes at scale. First, \emph{token-budget exhaustion}: when the true output length exceeds the generation budget, the predicted string is truncated, producing a spurious failure verdict regardless of model capability. Second, \emph{string-value prediction errors}: complex return types---floating-point numbers, nested dictionaries, sets with arbitrary ordering---require exact string reproduction, and minor formatting differences cause false rejections even when the model has correctly inferred the semantic output. Both failure modes grow more severe as code complexity increases from function-level to repository-level.

\textbf{Trajectory-level scoring}~\cite{zhang2025swerm}: Reward models predict binary patch-level correctness (resolved/unresolved) from the full code context and test suite. This formulation avoids generation altogether but discards per-test diagnostic information. A trajectory-level verdict of ``unresolved'' provides no signal about \emph{which} tests fail, precluding targeted re-repair strategies that could exploit failure localization. Automated repair agents~\cite{yang2024sweagent,xia2024agentless} operating on SWE-bench~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} could benefit from knowing which specific tests a candidate patch fails, but trajectory-level verifiers cannot provide this.

Neither paradigm explicitly addresses the formulation choice at the core of execution simulation: is open-ended generation necessary, or can a simpler classification formulation---predicting a single \textsc{pass}/\textsc{fail} token per test---suffice? We observe that the two CWM failure modes described above are artifacts of the generation formulation, not inherent to the task of execution simulation. Reformulating as per-test binary classification eliminates both by construction: the output is always a single token from a fixed vocabulary, independent of the complexity of the underlying execution output. However, this advantage is not universal. At function-level code where outputs are short and types are simple, generation encounters neither token exhaustion nor string mismatch---and classification provides no measurable benefit. The classification advantage emerges only beyond a complexity threshold where CWM failure modes activate.

Figure~\ref{fig:reformulation} illustrates the three formulations. We make the following contributions:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Complexity-dependent reformulation advantage.} We show that \cls{} and \cwm{} achieve near-equivalent accuracy at 4B on function-level code (gap 1.24\pp{}, 5 seeds), but the gap widens to 2.43\pp{} at 8B (3 matched seeds, $p = 0.0066$). From 4B to 8B, \cls{} gains +0.99\pp{} while \cwm{} loses $-$0.27\pp{}, indicating that additional model capacity benefits classification but not generation---consistent with the hypothesis that the string-prediction bottleneck, rather than model capacity, bounds CWM accuracy.

\item \textbf{Diagnostic granularity at equivalent accuracy.} Per-test classification achieves statistically equivalent variant-level accuracy to trajectory-level scoring (TOST equivalence test $p = 0.007$, $\pm$2\pp{} margin) while providing per-test diagnostic signals---which specific tests fail---at no accuracy cost. This enables downstream applications such as targeted re-repair that trajectory-level verifiers cannot support.

\item \textbf{Accuracy-utility frontier characterization.} Oracle analysis on SWE-bench Verified~\cite{chowdhury2024swebenchverified} shows that the per-test advantage concentrates in instances with $T \geq 2$ FAIL\_TO\_PASS tests (31\% of instances, contributing 55\% of total advantage), while instances with $T = 1$ (69\%) gain nothing from per-test granularity. This provides a practical decision framework for when per-test verification is worth deploying.
\end{itemize}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: \S\ref{sec:method} formalizes the three formulations and the oracle accuracy-utility framework, \S\ref{sec:experiments} presents experimental results, \S\ref{sec:related_work} discusses related work, and \S\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Execution Simulation for Code.}
Recent work has explored whether LLMs can simulate code execution without running the code.
Code World Models~\cite{meta2025cwm} mid-train a 32B LLM on execution traces to predict output strings given code and inputs, establishing the generation-based paradigm for execution simulation.
Self-Execution~\cite{ding2025selfexecution} extends this with step-by-step trace prediction and uses predicted outputs for self-verification of generated code.
CodeMind~\cite{liu2024codemind} provides a systematic framework for evaluating code reasoning capabilities along multiple dimensions including independent execution reasoning and dependent execution reasoning.
SolidCoder~\cite{chen2025solidcoder} addresses the gap between a model's mental simulation and actual execution by grounding generation in concrete execution feedback.
Ye et al.~\cite{ye2025demystifying} present an empirical analysis of error patterns in LLM execution simulation, identifying systematic failure modes in trace prediction.
All of these approaches formulate execution simulation as \emph{generation}---predicting output strings or execution traces. We reformulate the task as per-test binary classification and show that the choice of formulation interacts with code complexity: classification and generation achieve near-equivalent accuracy on simple function-level code, but classification scales better as complexity increases.

\paragraph{LLM-based Verification for Code Repair.}
Execution-free verification has emerged as a critical component for scaling test-time compute in code repair.
SWE-RM~\cite{zhang2025swerm} trains a 30B mixture-of-experts reward model that scores candidate patches at the trajectory level without execution, enabling execution-free ranking for best-of-$N$ selection.
Patch Reasoner~\cite{wu2025patchreasoner} uses explicit chain-of-thought reasoning to verify patch correctness, scaling verification through deeper reasoning rather than larger models.
Snell et al.~\cite{snell2024scaling} show that test-time compute scaling---generating multiple candidates and selecting via a verifier---can outperform parameter scaling, positioning verification accuracy as the key bottleneck.
S*~\cite{zhang2025sstar} proposes a hybrid test-time scaling strategy that combines execution-grounded selection with model-based scoring.
VG-Search~\cite{wang2025vgsearch} systematically studies how verification granularity affects compute-efficient test-time scaling, finding that finer-grained verification signals improve selection quality.
Our work contributes to this line by formally comparing per-test and trajectory-level granularity: we show that per-test classification achieves statistically equivalent patch-level accuracy to trajectory-level scoring (TOST $p = 0.007$) while additionally providing per-test diagnostic signals that trajectory-level verifiers discard.

\paragraph{Automated Program Repair.}
SWE-bench~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} established the standard benchmark for repository-level program repair, and SWE-bench Verified~\cite{chowdhury2024swebenchverified} provides a human-validated subset with higher label reliability.
Agent-based approaches such as SWE-agent~\cite{yang2024sweagent} use tool-augmented LLM agents to navigate repositories, localize faults, and generate patches.
Agentless~\cite{xia2024agentless} demonstrates that a simpler three-phase pipeline of localize--repair--validate can be competitive without agent scaffolding.
These systems rely on execution-based validation as the final filter, which is reliable but expensive at scale.
We focus specifically on the verification component: per-test classification provides failure-localized signals that could inform targeted re-repair strategies in these pipelines, a capability absent from trajectory-level verifiers.

\paragraph{Classification vs.\ Generation in NLP.}
The choice between classification and generation formulations is a recurring theme in NLP.
T5~\cite{raffel2020t5} systematically compares task formulations under a unified text-to-text framework, showing that framing affects performance even when model capacity is held constant.
BART~\cite{lewis2020bart} demonstrates generation--classification tradeoffs across summarization, question answering, and classification tasks.
In reading comprehension, SQuAD~\cite{rajpurkar2016squad} frames question answering as span extraction---a classification-style formulation---rather than open-ended generation, exploiting the constraint that answers are drawn from a fixed context.
We extend this formulation lens to code verification: where prior work finds that the optimal formulation depends on task structure, we identify \emph{code complexity} as the key moderator---classification and generation converge on simple code but diverge as complexity grows.

%
These results establish classification as a complexity-dependent alternative to generation-based execution simulation, offering a practical advantage that grows with model size and code complexity.
\end{abstract}
